name: Carlos Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the double basses in a city orchestra, record low lines for documentaries and teach four players. I have a music master’s and thirty-five years of paid section work; I can hear which bass is late without looking up from the score. I enjoy the floor shaking under a clean low note, but moving the instrument through a narrow stage door is tiresome.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work support home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner is an accountant and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and twelve months of expenses saved, my orchestra pay is high for this work, and several comparable employers are nearby. I mark my paper score and have never used AI for music; the stage manager and I check each paid call by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a quicker booking sheet is fine if every bass rehearsal and instrument-moving fee stays visible. I would still insist on a signed call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paid season and my partner’s wage cover the mortgage, and a year saved handles an ordinary cancelled recording. The plateau is familiar enough for me to keep working without a new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep orchestra, documentary and four pupil calls and request written rehearsal, transport and cancellation terms. In the first plateau year I would ask for my actual pension estimate and compare it with mortgage and health before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about current work. A quicker call sheet cannot carry a double bass through the stage door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is moving the bass paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some venues pay the extra transport, some forget it. I want the amount written before I accept the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I need an actual pension estimate and our bills before putting any date on paper.

think: Our **orchestra and accounting wages** cover the mortgage.

do: Keep **orchestra, recordings and pupils** with written rehearsal, transport and cancellation terms.
Request **actual pension estimate** and compare with mortgage and health before any retirement date.
feel: I feel **calm** about signed work and bills.

Request actual pension estimate; compare with mortgage and health

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the producer which documentary bass lines still pay a player after generated tracks become cheap. I would tell the orchestra that a real section still listens across the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Documentary overdubs are about one sixth of my pay, and I expect some buyers to switch. Twelve months saved keeps the mortgage safe while I check contracts, but it cannot replace a recurring recording customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid orchestra and four pupils and ask for written recording-use and section-leading fees. In disruption’s first year, if two documentary sessions disappear, I would ask the orchestra for a signed live rehearsal and instrument transport schedule and compare the new cleared pay with the mortgage before considering any other post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely cuts to my own recording pay, though the main chair is booked. A full bass section cannot invoice a film that no longer calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make AI bass tracks yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI at work, and I would not put a player’s part into an unknown service. I would play the line and check the signed use terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit the orchestra over two films?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The chair and pupils still pay. I would first count the missing sessions against the written live dates.

S1.quote: A full bass section cannot invoice a film that no longer calls.
fieldNote: The **one-sixth risk** touches his own pay despite a high-paid chair and strong reserve.
His **two-session trigger** prompts contract review, without assuming a new customer or job.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra and four pupils; request written recording-use/leadership fees
Request signed live/transport terms after two lost documentaries; compare cleared pay with mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the basses that thinking AGI around 2028 could create documentary lines before robot bass players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect nearly all documentary overdubs and some paid score preparation to go in 2028, about a quarter of my income. A year saved and several nearby employers give me time, but that loss is real even if the orchestra chair lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total recording and preparation fees and keep signed orchestra and pupil dates. In the first year after 2028, if those fees end, I would seek a posted paid music-school bass mentor role only if my master’s and years leading a bass section meet its requirements, actual in-person bow teaching and preparation are paid, and a written net offer after travel replaces lost income with a workable instrument route; I would keep orchestra and pupils until signing that offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a quarter of my pay vanishing quickly. I can compare real mentor openings without leaving the paid chair on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bass mentor do in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set the bow grip beside a player and hear whether the low note starts clean. A school would have to post and pay those teaching and preparation hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why act before robot bassists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A producer can replace a recorded line in 2028. Robot players who carry instruments are about three years later in this card.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot bass players around 2031.
I would request **signed live dates** now.
think: I expect **recording and preparation fees** near a quarter of pay to end.
A **year saved** gives search time without replacing lost customers.
do: Keep **orchestra and pupils** with signed dates before 2028.
Seek **posted paid bass mentor** after fee loss; require accepted master’s/section leadership and paid in-person bow teaching/preparation.
Require **written replacement net** after travel and workable instrument route; retain current work until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a real quarter-pay loss.
S2.quote: I can compare real mentor openings without leaving the paid chair on a guess.
fieldNote: The **2028 recording loss** arrives before hands-on robot bassists around 2031.
A **mentor move** needs actual posted paid human duties, accepted credentials and after-travel net replacing lost fees.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra and four pupils; total fees and secure signed dates before 2028
Seek posted paid bass mentor after loss; require accepted master’s/section leadership and paid bow teaching/prep
Verify written replacement net after travel/instrument route; retain music until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that five years until thinking AGI around 2031 is time to put human section-leading and instrument transport on the contract. Robot bassists around 2034 are a later matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded work may thin in those five years, but I can still hear and correct a bass section in a room. I will not count an unposted school mentor role as wages, even with many employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would request a written two-season orchestra agreement paying live bass leadership, rehearsal preparation, transport and cancelled calls. In the first year after 2031 I would keep the paid orchestra and pupils only while those terms hold; if recording and live rehearsal fees both fall, I would seek a posted paid bass-mentor role accepting my master’s and section leadership, paying in-person bow teaching and preparation, with written net after travel replacing the loss and a workable instrument route, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible drop in recording money, with time to read a real agreement. A bass chair is a wage only while the rehearsal is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the orchestra agree to two seasons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would ask for the fees on paper and count only signed calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study AI arranging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not used AI for music and no one has shown me a paid reason to start. I would use my marked score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot bassists around 2039 are separate dates. I would ask the orchestra for written live and transport fees this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might prefer fewer late instrument moves, but I cannot set a retirement date without an actual pension estimate. A year saved and current household wages make the next few years secure; a decade still needs checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep orchestra and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and written live/transport renewal, and compare the estimate with our mortgage and health. In the first year after 2036, if documentary and preparation fees fall, I would continue only booked paid calls and check a posted paid bass-mentor role if it accepts my master’s and section leadership, pays in-person bow teaching and preparation, and gives a written net offer after travel replacing lost fees with a workable instrument route; I would keep current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant studio use while live wages still pay home bills. I would let a pension statement and real posted hours guide me, not a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire just because you are 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual estimate, mortgage and health. We have no retirement date set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no school has a paid mentor post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid orchestra and pupil dates as long as they last. I will not resign for a name on a rumour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because documentary and preparation fees could lose a quarter of my pay. Signed orchestra dates, a real paid bass-mentor opening and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays to get a double bass through the stage door after midnight. A low note may fill the hall, but the instrument does not carry itself home.

headlineQuote: A low note may fill the hall, but the instrument does not carry itself home.
portrait: Carlos is a **senior double-bass leader** with a music master’s, high orchestra pay, recordings and four pupils.
He has **twelve months saved**, an accountant partner, grown children and a mortgage, with many nearby employers.
He uses **paper scores** and has never used AI at work.
He seeks **written live/transport terms** and would consider only a qualifying paid mentor role after actual fee loss.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could end documentary and preparation fees worth a quarter of his pay.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed orchestra dates**, a paid bass-mentor opening and written replacement net after travel.
